clinicalPearls: Infarction of a portion of the testis rather than the whole gland, presenting with acute testicular pain
It is an uncommon cause of the acute scrotum and an important mimic of testicular tumour on imaging
Many cases are idiopathic, though causes include epididymo-orchitis, trauma, sickle cell disease, vasculitis and hypercoagulable states
Ultrasound shows a wedge-shaped or rounded avascular area, and contrast-enhanced imaging confirms absent perfusion of the segment
The main concern is distinguishing it from a testicular neoplasm to avoid unnecessary orchidectomy
Where imaging is confident and tumour markers are normal, it can be managed conservatively with follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Segmental testicular infarction results from occlusion or compromise of a branch of the testicular vasculature supplying part of the testis, producing ischaemic necrosis of that segment while the rest of the gland remains perfused. Precipitants include local inflammation (epididymo-orchitis) causing vascular compression, trauma, sickling in sickle cell disease, vasculitis and thrombophilia, although many cases are idiopathic. The resulting focal avascular lesion can radiologically resemble a tumour, which is the key diagnostic challenge.
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and, where available, contrast-enhanced ultrasound
MRI in equivocal cases to characterise the lesion
Assessment for a hypercoagulable or vasculitic cause
Interval imaging to demonstrate a decreasing lesion supporting a benign diagnosis
redFlags: Imaging or markers suggesting a testicular tumour
An underlying thrombophilia or vasculitis needing treatment
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic segmental infarction generally has a benign course with the lesion shrinking over time, and the testis can often be preserved when malignancy is confidently excluded.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a tumour and performing unnecessary orchidectomy
Failing to use contrast imaging or follow-up to clarify the diagnosis
Overlooking an underlying prothrombotic or vasculitic cause
Confusing it with torsion or abscess
